prize_parts.citation: For the invention and realization of optical lattice clocks, in which magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms made frequency standards at the 1e-18 level possible.

statement.case_for: My preferred configuration is unchanged: B015 as a single-part prize to Katori and Ye. The round-1 exchange tested it from three directions and the core claim survived each. First, the invention: Katori's magic-wavelength lattice removes the light shift of the trapping field while keeping many neutral atoms in the Lamb-Dicke regime, which is a distinct concept from the frequency comb (2005) and from single-ion control (2012). The comb makes optical frequencies countable and the ion work controls one quantum system; the lattice clock is the way to interrogate many atoms at once and so to reach low statistical and systematic uncertainty together. Second, the realization: Ye's group took strontium to about 1e-18, with a millimetre-scale gravitational redshift resolved across a sample, and the result was reproduced at RIKEN/Tokyo, PTB, NIST, SYRTE and NPL with agreed comparisons, so the claim does not depend on one laboratory or on an interpretation that might still move. Third, the exchange showed convergence on the physics from members outside atomic physics (Mehlig, Olsson, Pearce moved to it; Eriksson now accepts it as first-rate), which answers Lindroth's fair warning that two of the first places came from atomic physicists. I weigh that as a check on my own bias, not as a vote count. I do not think the SI redefinition of the second is a precondition: the scientific case rests on demonstrated performance and on tests already done.
statement.case_against: The reservations from round 1 are not removed, only bounded. The comb and ion-control prizes are close in subject, so the citation has to name the neutral-atom lattice and the 1e-18 regime, and a committee could still call this refinement in kind. Danielsson's challenge stands in part: the clock is an enabling measurement, and what it has taught us about nature (redshift at millimetre scale, bounds on drifting constants, dark-matter searches) is real but is mostly limits and demonstrations rather than a new phenomenon. The credit boundary is also real: Lemonde and Le Targat in Paris, the PTB and NIST groups, Ludlow and Lemke, and the ion-clock community reached comparable accuracy by other routes, and the supplied names cannot represent them. I judge the line between concept (Katori) and the realization that proved it (Ye) to be the defensible one, but I cannot verify priority details beyond the supplied material. Finally, B006 is a larger field, and the committee should accept that a prize for B015 now leaves it for a later year because of an open mechanism, not because it is smaller.

responses.point: Danielsson holds B006 first as prediction followed by an unexpected experimental result, and asked what the lattice clock has taught us about nature rather than how precisely it measures; he keeps B015 as a second alternative and says he would not block it.
responses.response: That is the right test and I will answer it directly. The lattice clock has already given a resolved gravitational redshift over a millimetre, which is a laboratory test of general relativity at a length scale nobody could reach before. It has set tighter bounds on drifts of fundamental constants and on certain dark-matter couplings, and it has made many-body effects in a degenerate Fermi gas a controlled systematic rather than a nuisance. I concede these are mostly limits and demonstrations, not a surprise like superconductivity in carbon. Where we still differ is maturity: the correlated and superconducting phases in B006 are discovered, as you say, but I cannot write a citation that is safe against the open mechanism and against the Cao-group credit gap. I keep B006 as my first alternative and I would support it in a later year, and I do not accept that a measurement prize ranks below a discovery prize by category.

responses.point: Lindroth ranks B015 first but warns that two first places come from atomic physicists, treats overlap with the single-ion lineage as a possible incremental-in-kind judgment, and rejected my B010 companion idea because it is really two achievements.
responses.response: I accept her objection to B010. Cirac and Zoller, Blatt and the lattice-simulation strand are two achievements, and with a three-person limit any pairing would force a truncated credit list and reopen the attribution fights that make B015 attractive. I have dropped B010 from my alternatives for that reason and withdraw the two-part idea I floated. On the single-ion lineage I think the distinction is the one Mehlig drew: the ion clock rests on trapping and control already recognised in 2012, while the lattice clock has its own concept and error budget. I would still want the citation to say 'neutral atoms' so that no one reads it as excluding ion clocks by omission, and I share her caution that none of us has verified specific uncertainty records.

responses.point: Mehlig moved from B023 to B015, argues the SI redefinition must not be a precondition, and wants the citation separated from 2005 and 2012 while pairing only Katori and Ye.
responses.response: I agree with his answer on the redefinition and I have moved to it from my round-1 hedge. Tying merit to a metrological-body timetable would be a mistake, and the demonstrated performance, independent agreement and fundamental-physics tests are already in the record. I also agree that the pair should not be diluted by adding ion-clock names. Where I add something is the credit boundary he mentions in passing: Ye's group is credited for accuracy, but the Paris and PTB lattice work was contemporaneous, so the committee should say openly that the citation honours the concept and the first decisive realization, not every group that reached 1e-18. His comment on the KPZ credit gap also persuades me that B023 cannot be our alternative.

responses.point: Eriksson prefers B055, ranked B015 last in his opening, now treats it as his second alternative, and states that B015 beats B055 on clean credit but not on scientific reach.
responses.response: I appreciate the candid movement, and I take the scientific-reach point seriously, since B055 changed how a whole community of materials theorists works. The difference between us is how much weight the credit gap carries. In B055 the three supplied names omit Bernevig, Hughes, Zhang, Fu, Moore, Balents and Roy and the ARPES work, so the citation either has to be broad and contested or narrow and arbitrary. For B015 the two names correspond to the proposal and the realization, with a boundary I can describe. I have placed B055 among my alternatives because its maturity is real, and I would ask whether you see a three-name framing around the two-dimensional quantum spin Hall effect that does not leave the 3D generalization out.

responses.point: Olsson now ranks B015 first, wants the citation to name the invention and its realization at 1e-18 rather than metrology in general, and does not want Ye's many-body and redshift results read as a separate discovery.
responses.response: I agree entirely and I have rewritten my citation along those lines: invention of the lattice clock by magic-wavelength trapping of many neutral atoms, and its realization at 1e-18. I also agree that Ye's many-body and redshift measurements are consequences of the Katori concept, shown to work, and that they argue for the pair and not for a third name. My round-1 point that B013 has concentrated support still stands, but your move away from it shows the committee does not need a split prize here.

uncertainties: Whether the committee accepts the 'neutral-atom lattice' framing as distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes, or insists on a wording that also covers single-ion optical clocks.
How the Paris, PTB, NIST and other lattice-clock groups should be acknowledged in public material when only Katori and Ye are named; I cannot verify priority beyond the supplied evidence.
Whether the committee will be willing to leave B006 for a later year if the pairing mechanism remains unresolved, and whether that is consistent with how it treats B015.
My recollection of the clock literature and of specific uncertainty records is not independently verified.
statement.conflict_note: Unchanged from round 1. I spent a research stay in John Hall's laboratory in Boulder (Hall was recognised in 2005 for the frequency comb, which is adjacent to this field), and my own work in laser spectroscopy, quantum memories and quantum information at Lund, including WACQT and Deep Light Vision, makes B010 and quantum-sensing topics close to my area. My profile documents no personal or institutional tie to Katori, Ye or any credited name in B015, B006 or B055, so no specific recusal is warranted, and I disclose the Hall connection for the committee to judge. I note that no member has asked me to recuse, and I did not mention B010 in my preferred configuration.
